docs.title: DataReuploading: Complete Feature Demonstration¶
docs.text: Library: encoding-atlas Version: 0.2.0 Encoding: DataReuploading — A quantum feature map that repeatedly encodes classical data throughout the circuit, interleaved with entangling layers.

docs.title: Overview¶
docs.text:
Data re-uploading is a foundational technique in quantum machine learning. The key idea is to encode classical data multiple times throughout the circuit, interleaved with entangling layers. This creates quantum states with rich Fourier spectra, enabling high expressivity.

$$|\psi(x)\rangle = [U_{\text{ent}} \cdot U_{\text{data}}(x)]^L |0\rangle^{\otimes n}$$

where $U_{\text{data}}(x)$ encodes features via RY rotations and $U_{\text{ent}}$ provides entanglement via a CNOT ladder.

Key advantages:

  • High Expressivity — Multiple layers increase accessible Fourier frequencies
  • Universal Approximation — With trainable parameters, can approximate any continuous function
  • Hardware-Friendly — Only requires RY + CNOT gates with linear connectivity
  • Efficient Depth-Width Trade-off — Uses fewer qubits through cyclic feature mapping

References:

  1. Pérez-Salinas et al. (2020). "Data re-uploading for a universal quantum classifier." Quantum, 4, 226.
  2. Schuld, Sweke & Meyer (2021). "Effect of data encoding on the expressive power." Physical Review A, 103(3).
  3. Goto et al. (2021). "Universal approximation property." Physical Review Letters, 127(9).

This notebook demonstrates every feature of the DataReuploading encoding in the encoding-atlas library.

docs.title: 2. Creating a DataReuploading Encoding¶
docs.text:
The DataReuploading constructor accepts three parameters:

  • n_features (int, required): Number of classical features to encode
  • n_layers (int, default=3): Number of re-uploading layers
  • n_qubits (int or None, default=None): Number of qubits (defaults to n_features)

docs.title: 3. Constructor Validation¶
docs.text: The constructor validates all parameters strictly. Let's verify each validation rule.

docs.title: 4. Core Properties¶
docs.text: Every encoding provides fundamental properties inherited from BaseEncoding.

docs.title: 5. Depth Formula Deep Dive¶
docs.text:
The circuit depth is computed exactly:

$$\text{depth} = n_{\text{layers}} \times \left(\lceil \frac{n_{\text{features}}}{n_{\text{qubits}}} \rceil + (n_{\text{qubits}} - 1)\right)$$

  • Encoding sublayer depth: $\lceil n_{\text{features}} / n_{\text{qubits}} \rceil$ (cyclic feature mapping)
  • Entangling sublayer depth: $n_{\text{qubits}} - 1$ (CNOT ladder)

docs.title: 6. EncodingProperties¶
docs.text: The .properties attribute returns a frozen dataclass with comprehensive encoding metadata. It's computed lazily and cached (thread-safe).

docs.title: 7. Gate Count Breakdown¶
docs.text: The gate_count_breakdown() method returns a detailed dictionary of gate counts by type.

docs.title: 8. Resource Summary¶
docs.text: The resource_summary() method provides a comprehensive resource analysis including circuit structure, gate counts, encoding characteristics, hardware requirements, and recommendations.

docs.title: 9. Entanglement Pairs¶
docs.text: The get_entanglement_pairs() method returns the qubit pairs connected by CNOT gates. DataReuploading uses a linear (ladder) topology: (0,1), (1,2), ..., (n-2, n-1).

docs.title: 10. Circuit Generation — PennyLane Backend¶
docs.text: The PennyLane backend returns a callable function that applies gates when invoked within a QNode context.

docs.title: 11. Circuit Generation — Qiskit Backend¶
docs.text: The Qiskit backend returns a QuantumCircuit object.

docs.title: 12. Circuit Generation — Cirq Backend¶
docs.text: The Cirq backend returns a cirq.Circuit object.

docs.title: 13. Batch Circuit Generation¶
docs.text: The get_circuits() method generates circuits for multiple data samples, with optional parallel processing.

docs.title: 14. Input Validation¶
docs.text: The encoding validates all inputs comprehensively, catching errors early with clear messages.

docs.title: 15. Cyclic Feature Mapping¶
docs.text:
When n_features > n_qubits, features are mapped cyclically: feature $i$ maps to qubit $i \mod n_{\text{qubits}}$.

For example, with 6 features on 3 qubits:

  • Features 0, 3 → qubit 0
  • Features 1, 4 → qubit 1
  • Features 2, 5 → qubit 2

docs.title: 16. Single-Qubit Mode¶
docs.text: With n_qubits=1, DataReuploading creates a non-entangling but still expressive feature map. Even a single qubit can represent functions with $L$ Fourier frequencies when using $L$ layers — this is the key insight of data re-uploading.

docs.title: 17. Deep Circuit Warning¶
docs.text: When n_layers > 10, the constructor emits a UserWarning about potential trainability challenges (barren plateaus).

docs.title: 18. Statevector Simulation & Analysis¶
docs.text: The encoding_atlas.analysis module provides tools for simulating encodings and analyzing the resulting quantum states.

docs.title: 19. Partial Traces & Entanglement Inspection¶
docs.text: Examine the entanglement structure by tracing out qubits and computing local state properties.

docs.title: 20. Expressibility Analysis¶
docs.text: Expressibility measures how well an encoding covers the Hilbert space. Lower KL divergence = higher expressibility (closer to Haar-random).

docs.title: 21. Entanglement Capability¶
docs.text: Measures the encoding's ability to generate entanglement, using the Meyer-Wallach measure (0 = product state, 1 = maximally entangled).

docs.title: 22. Trainability Analysis¶
docs.text: Detects barren plateau risk by analyzing gradient variance. Higher variance = better trainability.

docs.title: 23. Simulability Analysis¶
docs.text: Determines whether the encoding can be efficiently simulated classically.

docs.title: 24. Resource Counting & Comparison¶
docs.text: Compare DataReuploading with other encodings using the analysis module's resource tools.

docs.title: 25. Capability Protocols¶
docs.text: The library uses runtime-checkable protocols to expose optional capabilities. This follows the Interface Segregation Principle — encodings only implement what makes sense for them.

docs.title: 26. Registry System¶
docs.text: Encodings can be created by name using the registry system.

docs.title: 27. Equality, Hashing & Collections¶
docs.text: Encodings support equality comparison and hashing, so they work in sets and as dictionary keys.

docs.title: 28. Serialization (Pickle)¶
docs.text: Encodings support pickle serialization for saving/loading. The thread lock is excluded during pickling and recreated during unpickling.

docs.title: 29. Thread Safety¶
docs.text:
DataReuploading is designed to be thread-safe:

  • Properties use double-checked locking for lazy initialization
  • Input validation creates defensive copies
  • Circuit generation is stateless

docs.title: 30. Logging & Debugging¶
docs.text: The module supports Python's standard logging for debugging circuit generation.

docs.title: 31. Comparison with Other Encodings¶
docs.text: Compare DataReuploading side-by-side with AngleEncoding and IQPEncoding.

docs.title: 32. Edge Cases¶
docs.text: Demonstrating that the library handles edge cases robustly.

docs.title: 33. Gradient Computation¶
docs.text: The analysis module provides parameter-shift rule based gradient computation.

docs.title: 34. Exception Hierarchy¶
docs.text: The library provides a rich exception hierarchy for precise error handling.

docs.title: Best Practices¶
docs.text:
1. Layer Selection: Start with n_layers=3 (default). Increase for complex functions, decrease if trainability is poor.
  2. Qubit Efficiency: Use n_qubits < n_features with cyclic mapping to reduce hardware requirements.
  3. Backend Choice: Use PennyLane for simulation, Qiskit for IBM hardware, Cirq for Google hardware.
  4. Input Scaling: Scale features to $[0, 2\pi]$ or $[-\pi, \pi]$ for best results.
  5. Trainability Monitoring: Keep n_layers \leq 10$ to avoid barren plateaus. Use the estimate_trainability()` tool to check.
  6. Universal Approximation: Add trainable parameters between data uploads for full universal approximation capability.
  7. Parallel Processing: Use parallel=True in get_circuits() for large batches (>100 samples).

docs.title: Mathematical Summary¶
docs.text:
$$\text{Circuit: } |\psi(x)\rangle = [U_{\text{CNOT}} \cdot \prod_i RY(x_i)]^L |0\rangle^{\otimes n}$$

$$\text{Depth: } d = L \times \left(\lceil n_f / n_q \rceil + (n_q - 1)\right)$$

$$\text{Gates: } G = L \times (n_f + \max(0, n_q - 1))$$

$$\text{Fourier frequencies: } \omega \in \{-L, \ldots, L\}$$

$$\text{Trainability: } T \approx \max(0.4, 0.9 - 0.05L)$$

  amplitude:
    Amplitude encoding provides exponential compression (4 qubits for 16 features)

  hamiltonian:

  hardware_efficient:
    Hardware-efficient encoding minimises gate decomposition overhead on real quantum devices

  higher_order_angle:
    Higher-order angle encoding captures polynomial feature interactions (order-k products) without entanglement

  iqp:
    IQP encoding creates highly entangled states with provable classical simulation hardness, well-suited for kernel methods

  pauli_feature_map:
    Pauli Feature Map enables configurable Pauli-string rotation structures for custom feature interactions

  qaoa:
    QAOA-inspired encoding uses cost-mixer layer structure suited for combinatorial and graph-structured problems

  so2_equivariant:
    SO(2) equivariant encoding guarantees mathematically rigorous 2D rotational equivariance for the 2-feature input

  swap_equivariant:
    Swap equivariant encoding guarantees rigorous S_2 pair-swap symmetry over feature pairs

  symmetry_inspired:
    Symmetry-inspired encoding provides a heuristic symmetry-aware inductive bias for the given problem

  trainable:
    Trainable encoding interleaves data rotations with learnable parameter layers for task-specific optimisation

    ZZ Feature Map provides standard pairwise feature interactions via (pi-x_i)(pi-x_j) phase encoding for kernel methods

docs.title: Encoding Atlas — Guide & Recommendation System¶
docs.text:
This notebook provides a comprehensive walkthrough of the encoding_atlas.guide module, which helps users select the best quantum data encoding for their problem.

The guide module has three components:

Component Purpose rules.py Knowledge base of 16 encodings with hard constraints and soft tags recommender.py Two-phase recommendation engine (hard filter → soft scoring) decision_tree.py Deterministic, interpretable decision tree for encoding selection

Table of Contents

  1. Setup & Imports
  2. The Knowledge Base — ENCODING_RULES
  3. Hard Constraint Filtering — get_matching_encodings()
  4. The Recommender — recommend_encoding()
  5. The Decision Tree — EncodingDecisionTree
  6. All 16 Encodings: Reachability Proof
  7. Decision Priority Hierarchy
  8. Parameter Deep-Dives
  9. Edge Cases & Robustness
  10. Recommender vs Decision Tree Comparison
  11. Real-World Scenarios
  12. Confidence Analysis
  13. Connecting Recommendations to Actual Encodings
  14. Summary

docs.title: 2. The Knowledge Base — ENCODING_RULES ¶
docs.text: The knowledge base is a dictionary mapping 16 canonical encoding names to their rule entries. Each entry is an EncodingRule TypedDict with 11 fields that describe when an encoding should (or shouldn't) be used.

docs.title: 2.1 EncodingRule Schema¶
docs.text: Each rule entry contains these 11 fields:

docs.title: 2.2 Exploring Encoding Categories¶
docs.text: Let's categorize all 16 encodings by their properties.

docs.title: 3. Hard Constraint Filtering — get_matching_encodings() ¶
docs.text:
The get_matching_encodings() function performs a two-phase check:

  1. Hard filter — eliminates encodings whose structural preconditions fail
  2. Soft match — among survivors, selects those whose best_for tags overlap with requirements and whose avoid_when tags don't overlap with constraints

docs.title: 3.5 Direct Hard Constraint Checking with _passes_hard_constraints()¶
docs.text: The internal _passes_hard_constraints() function checks whether a specific encoding's rule entry satisfies the user's structural requirements. It returns True if all 6 hard constraints pass.

docs.title: 4. The Recommender — recommend_encoding() ¶
docs.text:
The recommend_encoding() function is the main public API. It takes up to 10 parameters and returns a Recommendation dataclass with:

  • encoding_name: The top recommended encoding
  • explanation: Human-readable rationale
  • alternatives: Up to 3 runner-up encoding names
  • confidence: Score in [0, 1] indicating certainty

docs.title: 4.2 All 10 Parameters Explained¶
docs.text:
The recommender accepts 10 parameters:

# Parameter Type Default Description 1 n_features int (required) Number of input features 2 n_samples int 500 Number of training samples 3 task str "classification" ML task type 4 hardware str "simulator" Target hardware 5 priority str "accuracy" Optimization priority 6 data_type str "continuous" Nature of input features (keyword-only) 7 symmetry str|None None Known data symmetry (keyword-only) 8 trainable bool False Learnable parameters desired (keyword-only) 9 problem_structure str|None None Domain structure (keyword-only) 10 feature_interactions str|None None Desired interaction type (keyword-only)

docs.title: 4.10 Feature Count and Accuracy Fallback¶
docs.text:
When priority='accuracy' and no other strong signals, the feature count determines the recommendation:

  • ≤ 4 features → IQP
  • 5-8 features → ZZ Feature Map
  • > 8 features → Amplitude

docs.title: 4.13 Fallback Behavior¶
docs.text: When no encoding passes all hard constraints, the recommender falls back to angle encoding with low confidence.

docs.title: 5. The Decision Tree — EncodingDecisionTree ¶
docs.text: The decision tree provides a deterministic, interpretable encoding selection path. Unlike the recommender (which scores and ranks), the tree follows a single path and returns exactly one encoding.

docs.title: 6. All 16 Encodings: Reachability Proof ¶
docs.text: Every one of the 16 encodings must be reachable as the primary recommendation from both the recommender and the decision tree. Here we prove it.

docs.title: 7. Decision Priority Hierarchy ¶
docs.text:
Both the recommender and decision tree follow a 7-level priority hierarchy:

  1. Data type — binary/discrete → basis
  2. Symmetry — rotation/cyclic/permutation_pairs/general → equivariant encodings
  3. Trainable — True → trainable encoding
  4. Problem structure — combinatorial/physics_simulation → QAOA/Hamiltonian
  5. Feature interactions — polynomial/custom_pauli → higher_order_angle/pauli_feature_map
  6. Priority — speed/noise_resilience/trainability → angle/hardware_efficient/data_reuploading
  7. Feature count — (accuracy fallback) ≤ 4/5-8/>8 → IQP/ZZ Feature Map/Amplitude

Higher levels always override lower levels.

docs.title: 10. Recommender vs Decision Tree Comparison ¶
docs.text: Feature Recommender Decision Tree Output Ranked list + confidence Single encoding Method Hard filter + soft scoring Deterministic if/elif chain Alternatives Up to 3 None Confidence 0.0-1.0 N/A Explanation Template-based N/A Parameters 10 7

docs.title: 11. Real-World Scenarios ¶
docs.text: Let's walk through realistic use cases to demonstrate how the recommendation system guides encoding selection.

docs.title: 12. Confidence Analysis ¶
docs.text: The confidence score maps raw suitability scores to a human-interpretable value in [0.50, 0.95].

docs.title: 13. Connecting Recommendations to Actual Encodings ¶
docs.text: The canonical names returned by the recommender and decision tree match the encoding registry keys. This means you can directly instantiate the recommended encoding using get_encoding().

docs.title: What We Covered¶
docs.text:
1. Knowledge Base (ENCODING_RULES): 16 encodings with 11 typed fields each, including hard constraints and soft tags
  2. Hard Constraint Filtering: 6 binary constraint gates that eliminate structurally invalid encodings
  3. Tag-Based Matching (get_matching_encodings()): Combining hard filters with soft best_for/avoid_when tag matching
  4. The Recommender (recommend_encoding()): 10-parameter API producing ranked recommendations with confidence scores
  5. The Decision Tree (EncodingDecisionTree): Deterministic 7-level tree for interpretable encoding selection
  6. Reachability: All 16 encodings are reachable as primary recommendation from both systems
  7. Priority Hierarchy: Higher-level decision criteria always override lower levels
  8. Parameter Deep-Dives: Every parameter's effect on the recommendation
  9. Edge Cases: Extreme feature counts, wrong symmetry+feature combos, conflicting constraints
  10. Consistency: Recommender and decision tree agree for canonical trigger parameters
  11. Real-World Scenarios: 10 practical use cases demonstrating the system
  12. Confidence Analysis: Scoring internals, confidence bands, and monotonicity
  13. Registry Integration: End-to-end from recommendation to instantiated encoding

docs.title: Key Design Properties¶
docs.text:
• Safety: Hard constraints are never violated — no encoding is ever recommended when its preconditions fail
  • Completeness: All 16 encodings are reachable from both the recommender and decision tree
  • Backward Compatibility: The original 5-positional-arg API still works unchanged
  • Interpretability: Every recommendation comes with an explanation and confidence score
  • Extensibility: Adding a 17th encoding requires only adding an entry to ENCODING_RULES, a leaf in the decision tree, and an explanation template

# Demonstrate pair count formulas

    enc_full = HamiltonianEncoding(n_features=n, entanglement='full', reps=1)
    enc_lin = HamiltonianEncoding(n_features=n, entanglement='linear', reps=1)
    enc_circ = HamiltonianEncoding(n_features=n, entanglement='circular', reps=1)

    n_full = len(enc_full.get_entanglement_pairs())
    n_lin = len(enc_lin.get_entanglement_pairs())
    n_circ = len(enc_circ.get_entanglement_pairs())

    expected_full = n * (n - 1) // 2
    expected_lin = n - 1
    expected_circ = n if n > 2 else n - 1

    print(
        f"n={n:>2}: full={n_full:>3} (exp={expected_full:>3}), "
        f"linear={n_lin:>2} (exp={expected_lin:>2}), "
        f"circular={n_circ:>2} (exp={expected_circ:>2})"
    )
    assert n_full == expected_full
    assert n_lin == expected_lin
    assert n_circ == expected_circ

def analyze_encoding(encoding):
    """Analyze any encoding using its capabilities."""
    info = {"class": type(encoding).__name__}

    if isinstance(encoding, ResourceAnalyzable):
        summary = encoding.resource_summary()
        info["n_qubits"] = summary["n_qubits"]
        info["depth"] = summary["depth"]
        info["total_gates"] = summary["gate_counts"]["total"]

    if isinstance(encoding, EntanglementQueryable):
        pairs = encoding.get_entanglement_pairs()
        info["n_pairs"] = len(pairs)

    return info

    def compute_kernel_matrix(encoding, X):
        """Compute the quantum kernel matrix for a dataset."""
        n_samples = X.shape[0]

        # Get all statevectors
        statevectors = []
        for i in range(n_samples):
            sv = get_statevector(encoding, X[i])
            statevectors.append(sv)

        # Compute kernel matrix
        K = np.zeros((n_samples, n_samples))
        for i in range(n_samples):
            for j in range(n_samples):
                K[i, j] = np.abs(np.vdot(statevectors[i], statevectors[j]))**2

        return K

    # Create a small dataset
    rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
    X_kernel = rng.uniform(0, 1, size=(6, 3))

    enc = HamiltonianEncoding(n_features=3, hamiltonian_type='iqp', reps=2)
    K = compute_kernel_matrix(enc, X_kernel)

    print("Quantum Kernel Matrix (IQP, 6 samples):")
    print(np.array2string(K, precision=4, suppress_small=True))

    # Verify kernel properties
    print(f"\nDiagonal elements (should be 1.0): {np.diag(K)}")
    print(f"Symmetric: {np.allclose(K, K.T)}")
    print(f"All eigenvalues >= 0 (PSD): {np.all(np.linalg.eigvalsh(K) >= -1e-10)}")

docs.title: Hamiltonian Encoding — Comprehensive Usage Guide¶
docs.text: Library: encoding-atlas Encoding: HamiltonianEncoding Version: 0.2.0

docs.title: What is Hamiltonian Encoding?¶
docs.text:
Hamiltonian encoding maps classical data into quantum states through time evolution under a data-dependent Hamiltonian operator:

$$|\psi(x)\rangle = e^{-iH(x)t} |+\rangle^{\otimes n}$$

where:

  • $|+\rangle = H|0\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|0\rangle + |1\rangle)$ is the equal superposition state
  • $H(x)$ is a data-dependent Hamiltonian
  • $t$ is the evolution time
  • $n$ is the number of qubits (one per feature)

The time evolution is approximated using Trotterization:

$$e^{-iH(x)t} \approx \left[\prod_j e^{-ic_j(x)\frac{t}{r}P_j}\right]^r$$

where $r$ is the number of Trotter steps (reps).

docs.title: Why Hamiltonian Encoding?¶
docs.text:
• Physics-motivated design: Grounded in quantum dynamics, providing natural inductive bias for physics-related ML tasks
  • Flexible Hamiltonian types: Choose from IQP, XY, Heisenberg, or Pauli-Z interaction structures
  • Rich entanglement: Creates highly entangled quantum states via configurable two-qubit interactions
  • Expressivity control: The evolution_time parameter provides explicit control over encoding strength
  • Not classically simulable: Potential for quantum advantage in kernel-based methods

docs.title: 2. Basic Instantiation & Defaults¶
docs.text: The simplest way to create a Hamiltonian encoding is to specify only n_features. All other parameters have sensible defaults.

docs.title: 3. Hamiltonian Types Deep Dive¶
docs.text:
The library supports four Hamiltonian types, each defining a different interaction structure:

Type Hamiltonian Interactions Gate Overhead 'iqp' $\sum_i x_i Z_i + \sum_{ij} (\pi - x_i)(\pi - x_j) Z_i Z_j$ ZZ only Lowest 'pauli_z' Same as IQP ZZ only Lowest 'xy' $\sum_{ij} (\pi - x_i)(\pi - x_j)(X_iX_j + Y_iY_j)$ XX + YY Medium 'heisenberg' $\sum_{ij} (\pi - x_i)(\pi - x_j)(X_iX_j + Y_iY_j + Z_iZ_j)$ XX + YY + ZZ Highest

docs.title: 3.1 IQP / Pauli-Z Type¶
docs.text:
The IQP (Instantaneous Quantum Polynomial) type uses diagonal Hamiltonians with Z and ZZ terms. It is the default type.

Gate decomposition per ZZ interaction:

  • CNOT → RZ → CNOT (depth 3, 2 CNOTs + 1 RZ)

pauli_z is functionally identical to iqp but provides a more explicit name.

docs.title: 3.2 XY Type¶
docs.text:
The XY model uses XX + YY interactions, creating coherent superpositions.

Gate decompositions:

  • XX: H⊗H → CNOT → RZ → CNOT → H⊗H (depth 5)
  • YY: Sdg⊗Sdg → H⊗H → CNOT → RZ → CNOT → H⊗H → S⊗S (depth 7)

The include_single_qubit_terms parameter controls whether $\sum_i x_i Z_i$ terms are added.

docs.title: 3.3 Heisenberg Type¶
docs.text: The most expressive type: combines XX + YY + ZZ interactions. This corresponds to the full isotropic Heisenberg model.

docs.title: 4. Entanglement Topologies¶
docs.text:
Three entanglement patterns are supported:

Topology Pairs Scaling Hardware Best For 'full' All (i,j) where i<j O(n²) All-to-all Max expressivity 'linear' (i, i+1) only O(n) Nearest-neighbor NISQ devices 'circular' Linear + (n-1, 0) O(n) Ring Periodic problems

docs.title: 5. Circuit Generation — Multi-Backend Support¶
docs.text:
Hamiltonian encoding supports three quantum computing backends:

  • PennyLane (default): Returns a callable closure
  • Qiskit: Returns a QuantumCircuit object
  • Cirq: Returns a cirq.Circuit object

docs.title: 5.4 Visualizing All Four Hamiltonian Types as Qiskit Circuits¶
6. Batch Processing & Memory-Efficient Iteration¶
docs.text:
The library offers three ways to process multiple samples:

  1. get_circuits() — Returns a list of all circuits
  2. get_circuits(..., parallel=True) — Parallel batch processing
  3. iter_circuits() — Memory-efficient generator

docs.title: 7.1 evolution_time — Encoding Strength¶
docs.text: The evolution time $t$ scales all rotation angles uniformly. Larger values create more complex states but may lead to harder optimization landscapes.

docs.title: 7.2 reps — Trotter Steps¶
docs.text: Higher reps improves the Trotterization accuracy but increases circuit depth linearly.

docs.title: 7.3 max_pairs — Limiting Two-Qubit Interactions¶
docs.text: For large systems with full entanglement, max_pairs limits the number of interaction pairs to control circuit depth.

docs.title: 7.4 include_single_qubit_terms¶
docs.text: For IQP and Pauli-Z, single-qubit Z rotations are always included (this parameter is ignored). For XY and Heisenberg, this controls whether $\sum_i x_i Z_i$ terms are added.

docs.title: 8. Properties & Resource Analysis¶
docs.text: Each encoding computes and caches an EncodingProperties dataclass with theoretical circuit properties.

docs.title: 9. Gate Count Analysis (Upper-Bound vs Exact)¶
docs.text:
The library distinguishes between:

  • gate_count_breakdown(): Upper-bound estimates (no input data needed)
  • count_gates(x): Exact counts for specific input (skips zero-angle gates)

docs.title: 10. Capability Protocols¶
docs.text: The library uses Python's structural subtyping (protocols) to check encoding capabilities at runtime.

docs.title: 11. Registry System¶
docs.text: All encodings are registered in a global registry and can be accessed by name.

docs.title: 12. Serialization & Deep Copy¶
docs.text: HamiltonianEncoding supports pickling (for distributed computing) and deep copying.

docs.title: 13. Equality, Hashing & Collections¶
docs.text: HamiltonianEncoding instances are hashable and support equality comparison based on all configuration parameters. This allows using them as dictionary keys and in sets.

docs.title: 14. Edge Cases & Robustness¶
docs.text: This section demonstrates that the library handles various edge cases gracefully.

docs.title: 14.3 Very Small and Very Large Inputs¶
14.5 Numpy Types for Parameters¶
docs.text: Most parameters (reps, max_pairs, evolution_time) accept numpy numeric types natively. However, n_features goes through BaseEncoding.__init__ which requires a Python int. Wrap it with int() if coming from numpy.

docs.title: 15. Input Validation & Error Handling¶
docs.text: The library validates all inputs and provides clear error messages.

docs.title: 16. Critical Point at π & Data Preprocessing¶
docs.text:
The two-qubit rotation angle uses the formula:

$$\text{angle} = \text{time\_step} \times (\pi - x_i)(\pi - x_j)$$

This has a critical point at $x = \pi$ where interactions vanish. The library warns you about this.

docs.title: 17. Rotation Angle Mathematics¶
docs.text: Understanding the rotation angle formulas is key to using Hamiltonian encoding effectively.

docs.title: 18. Depth Computation & Parallelization¶
docs.text:
Circuit depth is computed exactly using graph coloring for parallelization of two-qubit gates.

Two-qubit gates on disjoint qubit pairs can execute in parallel. The number of parallel groups (colors) depends on the entanglement topology:

Topology Parallel Groups Formula Linear 2 Always 2 (odd/even pairs) Circular 2 or 3 2 if n even, 3 if n odd Full n-1 or n n-1 if n even, n if n odd

docs.title: 19. Statevector Simulation & Verification¶
docs.text: Verify that the Hamiltonian encoding produces valid quantum states and that different configurations produce distinct states.

docs.title: 20. Quantum Kernel Computation¶
docs.text:
A key use case for Hamiltonian encoding is computing quantum kernels:

$$k(x, x') = |\langle \psi(x) | \psi(x') \rangle|^2$$

docs.title: 21. Comparing Hamiltonian Types Empirically¶
docs.text: Let's compare all four Hamiltonian types across multiple dimensions.

docs.title: Constructor Parameters¶
docs.text:
HamiltonianEncoding(
    n_features: int,                              # Required: 1+
    hamiltonian_type: str = 'iqp',                # 'iqp', 'pauli_z', 'xy', 'heisenberg'
    evolution_time: float = 1.0,                  # Any finite float (incl. negative)
    reps: int = 2,                                # >= 1 (Trotter steps)
    entanglement: str = 'full',                   # 'full', 'linear', 'circular'
    insert_barriers: bool = True,                 # Qiskit-only barriers
    max_pairs: int | None = None,                 # Limit entanglement pairs
    include_single_qubit_terms: bool = True,      # Z_i terms (XY/Heisenberg only)
)

docs.title: Rotation Angle Formulas¶
docs.text:
• Single-qubit: $\text{angle} = \frac{t}{r} \cdot x_i$
  • Two-qubit: $\text{angle} = \frac{t}{r} \cdot (\pi - x_i)(\pi - x_j)$

docs.title: Data Preprocessing¶
docs.text:
• Recommended: Scale features to $[0, 1]$ or $[-1, 1]$
  • Avoid: Ranges including $\pi \approx 3.14159$ in the interior
  • Zero features: Produce zero single-qubit rotation (gates skipped)
  • Features = $\pi$: Produce zero two-qubit interaction (critical point)

docs.title: Hardware-Efficient Encoding - Comprehensive Guide¶
docs.text:
This notebook provides a complete walkthrough of HardwareEfficientEncoding from the Quantum Encoding Atlas library. It covers every feature, parameter, method, and edge case.

Hardware-efficient encoding is a quantum data encoding technique designed for NISQ (Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum) devices. It uses only native gates (single-qubit rotations + CNOT) and respects physical qubit connectivity constraints, minimizing gate decomposition overhead and reducing circuit depth.

The encoding creates quantum states using:

$$|\psi(x)\rangle = \left[U_{\text{ent}} \cdot U_{\text{rot}}(x)\right]^{\text{reps}} |0\rangle^{\otimes n}$$

where $U_{\text{rot}}$ applies data-dependent rotations and $U_{\text{ent}}$ provides entanglement using connectivity-respecting CNOT gates.

docs.title: 1. Installation & Imports¶
docs.text: Install the library from PyPI and its optional backend dependencies.

docs.title: 2. Basic Instantiation¶
docs.text: HardwareEfficientEncoding requires only n_features (the number of classical features to encode). Each feature maps to one qubit.

docs.title: 3.1 n_features - Number of Classical Features¶
docs.text: Determines the number of qubits (1:1 mapping). Must be a positive integer.

docs.title: 3.2 reps - Number of Layer Repetitions¶
docs.text: Controls how many times the rotation + entanglement layers are repeated. Higher values increase expressivity but also circuit depth and accumulated errors. Must be a positive integer (>= 1).

docs.title: 3.3 rotation - Rotation Axis¶
docs.text:
Determines the single-qubit rotation gate used for data encoding. Must be one of "X", "Y", or "Z" (case-sensitive).

Rotation Gate Hardware Notes "X" RX(x) Native on most superconducting qubits "Y" RY(x) Default; creates real-valued amplitudes "Z" RZ(x) Often "virtual" with zero error on superconducting devices

docs.title: 3.4 entanglement - CNOT Topology¶
docs.text:
Controls the pattern of CNOT gates for entanglement. Must be one of "linear", "circular", or "full".

Topology Pairs (n=4) Count Best For "linear" (0,1), (1,2), (2,3) n-1 Superconducting (IBM, Google) "circular" (0,1), (1,2), (2,3), (3,0) n Ring topologies "full" All pairs where i < j n(n-1)/2 Ion traps (IonQ, Quantinuum)

docs.title: 4.2 Configuration Dictionary¶
docs.text: The config property returns a read-only copy of the encoding's configuration parameters.

docs.title: 5. Entanglement Topologies¶
docs.text: A detailed look at how each entanglement topology generates CNOT pairs.

docs.title: 5.1 Linear Entanglement¶
docs.text:
Nearest-neighbor connectivity: CNOT gates connect consecutive qubits. Creates n-1 pairs per layer.

q0 --[RY(x0)]--*-----------[RY(x0)]--*-----------
                |                      |
q1 --[RY(x1)]--X--*--------[RY(x1)]--X--*--------
                   |                      |
q2 --[RY(x2)]-----X--*-----[RY(x2)]-----X--*-----
                      |                      |
q3 --[RY(x3)]---------X----[RY(x3)]---------X----
     |--- rep 1 ---|        |--- rep 2 ---|

docs.title: 5.2 Circular Entanglement¶
docs.text: Linear connectivity plus a wrap-around CNOT from the last to the first qubit. Creates n pairs per layer (for n > 2).

docs.title: 5.3 Full Entanglement¶
docs.text: All-to-all connectivity: CNOT between every pair of qubits (i, j) where i < j. Creates n(n-1)/2 pairs per layer (O(n^2) scaling).

docs.title: 5.4 Entanglement Pair Immutability¶
docs.text: get_entanglement_pairs() returns a copy of the internal list, so modifying it doesn't affect the encoding.

docs.title: 6. Circuit Generation - Single Sample¶
docs.text: Use get_circuit(x, backend) to generate a quantum circuit for a single data sample.

docs.title: 6.1 Input Formats¶
docs.text: get_circuit accepts multiple input formats: numpy arrays, lists, tuples, and 2D arrays with a single row.

docs.title: 7. Circuit Generation - Batch Processing¶
docs.text: Use get_circuits(X, backend, parallel, max_workers) to generate circuits for multiple data samples.

docs.title: 8. Multi-Backend Support¶
docs.text: Hardware-efficient encoding supports three quantum computing frameworks: PennyLane, Qiskit, and Cirq.

docs.title: 9.1 Gate Count Breakdown¶
docs.text: gate_count_breakdown() returns a detailed dictionary of gate counts by type.

docs.title: 9.2 Resource Summary¶
docs.text: resource_summary() returns a comprehensive dictionary with circuit structure, gate counts, encoding characteristics, and hardware requirements.

docs.title: 9.3 Resource Scaling Formulas¶
docs.text: Resource Linear Circular Full Qubits n n n Circuit Depth 2r 2r 2r Single-qubit gates n*r n*r n*r Two-qubit gates (n-1)*r n*r n(n-1)/2*r Parameters n*r n*r n*r

docs.title: 10. Encoding Properties (EncodingProperties)¶
docs.text: The properties attribute returns a frozen (immutable) EncodingProperties dataclass with comprehensive encoding information. It is lazily computed on first access and cached (thread-safe).

docs.title: 11. Capability Protocols¶
docs.text: The library uses PEP 544 Protocols (structural subtyping) to define optional capabilities. HardwareEfficientEncoding satisfies both ResourceAnalyzable and EntanglementQueryable.

docs.title: 12. Analysis Tools¶
docs.text: The encoding_atlas.analysis module provides quantitative analysis functions that work with any encoding.

docs.title: 13. Input Validation & Edge Cases¶
docs.text: The library provides comprehensive input validation with clear error messages.

docs.title: 13.4 Single-Qubit Edge Case¶
docs.text: With n_features=1, the encoding has no entanglement and is classically simulable.

docs.title: 13.5 Two-Qubit Edge Case¶
docs.text: With n_features=2, linear and circular topologies produce identical entanglement pairs.

docs.title: 13.6 Rotation Gate Periodicity (2pi)¶
docs.text: Rotation gates are 2pi-periodic: R(theta) = R(theta + 2pik). Values outside the typical range still work, but a debug log is emitted.

docs.title: 13.7 Large Qubit Count Warnings¶
docs.text: The encoding warns when using non-linear topologies with more than 20 qubits.

docs.title: 13.8 Input Immutability¶
docs.text: The encoding creates defensive copies of input data, ensuring thread safety.

docs.title: 14.2 Hashing (Usable as Dict Keys and in Sets)¶
15. Thread Safety¶
docs.text: HardwareEfficientEncoding is designed for safe concurrent use.

docs.title: 16. Logging & Debugging¶
docs.text: The module uses Python's standard logging framework for debugging.

docs.title: 17. Comparison with Other Encodings¶
docs.text: Compare HardwareEfficientEncoding with other encodings from the library.

docs.title: 18.1 NISQ Hardware Deployment (Superconducting Qubits)¶
docs.text: Linear entanglement with RZ rotations minimizes errors on superconducting devices.

docs.title: 18.2 Ion Trap Deployment¶
docs.text: Full entanglement exploits the all-to-all connectivity of ion trap devices.

docs.title: 18.4 Comparing Rotation Axes on the Same Data¶
Summary¶
docs.text:
This notebook demonstrated every feature of HardwareEfficientEncoding from the Quantum Encoding Atlas library:

Core Features:

  • Constructor with 4 parameters: n_features, reps, rotation, entanglement
  • Three rotation axes (RX, RY, RZ) and three entanglement topologies (linear, circular, full)
  • Circuit generation for single samples (get_circuit) and batches (get_circuits)
  • Multi-backend support: PennyLane, Qiskit, Cirq

Analysis & Introspection:

  • Resource analysis: gate_count_breakdown(), resource_summary()
  • Encoding properties: properties (lazy, thread-safe, cached EncodingProperties)
  • Capability protocols: ResourceAnalyzable, EntanglementQueryable
  • Analysis module: count_resources, check_simulability, compare_resources, simulate_encoding_statevector, etc.

Robustness:

  • Comprehensive input validation (shape, dtype, NaN/Inf, complex numbers, strings)
  • Thread-safe design (defensive copies, double-checked locking)
  • Pickle serialization with full state preservation
  • Equality and hashing for use in sets and dicts
  • Warnings for large qubit counts with non-linear topologies
  • Configurable logging for debugging

Edge Cases:

  • Single qubit (n=1): no entanglement, classically simulable
  • Two qubits (n=2): all topologies equivalent
  • 2pi periodicity of rotation gates
  • Zero input encodes |0...0>
  • Large qubit warnings (n > 20)

docs.title: Overview¶
docs.text:
This notebook is the definitive guide to HigherOrderAngleEncoding from the encoding-atlas library. It demonstrates every constructor parameter, property, method, backend, edge case, and integration point.

What is Higher-Order Angle Encoding?

Standard angle encoding maps each feature $x_i$ to a rotation $R_Y(x_i)$ on qubit $i$. Higher-Order Angle Encoding generalises this by computing polynomial interaction terms — products like $x_i \cdot x_j$ (second-order) or $x_i \cdot x_j \cdot x_k$ (third-order) — and distributing them across qubits.

The rotation angle for each qubit is the sum of all terms assigned to it (scaled by a configurable factor):

$$\theta_q = s \cdot \sum_{T \in \mathcal{T}_q} \prod_{i \in T} x_i$$

where $s$ is the scaling factor and $\mathcal{T}_q$ is the set of polynomial terms assigned to qubit $q$ via round-robin distribution.

Key Properties:

  • Creates feature interactions without entangling gates → product state

  • Classically simulable (useful when combined with entangling ansatz layers)

  • Supports three rotation axes (X, Y, Z), two combination methods (product, sum), configurable order, scaling, and repetitions

docs.text:
HigherOrderAngleEncoding accepts the following parameters:

Parameter Type Default Description n_features int (required) Number of classical input features (≥ 1) order int 2 Maximum polynomial order (1 to n_features) rotation str 'Y' Rotation axis: 'X', 'Y', or 'Z' combination str 'product' Feature combination: 'product' or 'sum' include_first_order bool True Whether to include single-feature terms scaling float 1.0 Scaling factor for all rotation angles reps int 1 Number of circuit repetitions

docs.title: 4. Polynomial Term Generation & Assignment¶
docs.text:
Terms are generated in lexicographic order by degree, then assigned to qubits using round-robin by term index:

$$\text{qubit\_idx} = \text{term\_index} \mod n\_\text{qubits}$$

docs.title: 5. Rotation Angle Computation¶
docs.text: The compute_angles() method reveals the rotation angle each qubit will receive for a given input.

docs.title: 6. Circuit Generation — PennyLane Backend¶
docs.text: The PennyLane backend returns a callable function that applies rotation gates when called inside a QNode.

docs.title: 7. Circuit Generation — Qiskit Backend¶
docs.text: The Qiskit backend returns a QuantumCircuit object.

docs.title: 8. Circuit Generation — Cirq Backend¶
docs.text: The Cirq backend returns a cirq.Circuit object.

docs.title: 9. Batch Circuit Generation & Parallel Processing¶
docs.text: get_circuits() generates circuits for multiple input samples at once.

docs.title: 10. Gate Count Breakdown¶
docs.text: gate_count_breakdown() returns a typed dictionary with detailed gate counts.

docs.title: 11. Resource Summary¶
docs.text: resource_summary() provides a comprehensive view of circuit resources, polynomial configuration, and hardware requirements.

docs.title: 12. EncodingProperties (Base Class)¶
docs.text: The properties attribute returns a frozen EncodingProperties dataclass computed from the encoding configuration. It is lazily computed and cached (thread-safe).

docs.title: 13. Capability Protocols¶
docs.text: The library uses structural subtyping protocols (PEP 544) to define optional capabilities. You can check at runtime what an encoding supports.

docs.title: 14. Registry & Factory Access¶
docs.text: Encodings are registered under string names for factory-style creation.

docs.title: 15. Encoding Guide & Recommendations¶
docs.text: The library includes a recommendation system to help choose encodings.

docs.title: 18. Serialization (Pickle)¶
docs.text: Encodings support full pickle serialization, including cached properties.

docs.text: The encoding is immutable after construction — all read operations (including circuit generation) are thread-safe.

This notebook demonstrated every feature of HigherOrderAngleEncoding from the encoding-atlas library:

Category Features Covered Constructor All 7 parameters, defaults, case-insensitive normalization Validation Type errors, value errors, degenerate cases, input validation (NaN, Inf, shape, complex, string) Properties n_qubits, depth, n_terms, terms, config, properties (frozen, cached, thread-safe) Term System Generation, round-robin assignment, get_term_info(), with/without first-order Angles compute_angles(), product vs sum, scaling, manual verification Backends PennyLane (callable), Qiskit (QuantumCircuit), Cirq (Circuit), case-insensitive, None default Batching get_circuits(), sequential & parallel, max_workers, 1D input handling Resources gate_count_breakdown(), resource_summary(), EncodingProperties.to_dict() Protocols ResourceAnalyzable, EntanglementQueryable, DataTransformable, type guards Registry get_encoding("higher_order_angle", ...), list_encodings() Guide recommend_encoding() Equality __eq__, __hash__, sets, dict keys Repr __repr__ with all parameters Serialization pickle roundtrip with properties preservation Thread Safety Concurrent circuit generation, concurrent property access Edge Cases Single feature, zero input, negative/mixed values, extreme magnitudes, machine epsilon, near-pi Numerical Large scaling, high-order stability, all-zeros, product state normalization Comparisons product vs sum, with/without first-order, scaling sweep Utilities count_terms() standalone function, logging/debugging Visualization compare_encodings() Analysis Resources, simulability, Clifford/matchgate checks, entanglement bounds, cross-encoding comparison Cross-Backend State fidelity verification across PennyLane, Qiskit, and Cirq

Key Takeaways:

  1. Higher-Order Angle Encoding creates polynomial feature interactions without entanglement

  2. The resulting quantum state is always a product state → classically simulable

  3. It is most useful when combined with entangling ansatz layers in variational circuits

  4. The library provides comprehensive validation, thread safety, and multi-backend support

  5. All resource analysis and comparison tools work seamlessly with this encoding

def analyze_encoding(enc):
    """Generic function that works with any encoding."""
    info = {"name": repr(enc)}

    if isinstance(enc, ResourceAnalyzable):
        summary = enc.resource_summary()
        info["total_gates"] = summary["gate_counts"]["total"]
        info["is_entangling"] = summary["is_entangling"]

    if isinstance(enc, EntanglementQueryable):
        pairs = enc.get_entanglement_pairs()
        info["entanglement_pairs"] = len(pairs)
    else:
        info["entanglement_pairs"] = "N/A (not entangling)"

    if isinstance(enc, DataTransformable):
        info["has_transform"] = True
    else:
        info["has_transform"] = False

    return info

result = analyze_encoding(enc)
print("=== Generic analysis via protocols ===")

docs.title: IQPEncoding: Complete Feature Demonstration¶
docs.text:
Library: encoding-atlas Version: 0.2.0 Author: Ashutosh Mishra

This notebook provides an exhaustive, hands-on demonstration of IQPEncoding from the Quantum Encoding Atlas library. IQPEncoding implements Instantaneous Quantum Polynomial (IQP) circuits for quantum machine learning, creating highly entangled quantum states with provable classical hardness guarantees.

docs.title: Mathematical Background¶
docs.text:
IQP encoding creates quantum states of the form:

$$|\psi(\mathbf{x})\rangle = U_{\text{IQP}}(\mathbf{x})|0\rangle^{\otimes n}$$

where $U_{\text{IQP}}$ consists of alternating layers (repeated reps times) of:

  1. Hadamard layer: $H^{\otimes n}$ creates uniform superposition
  2. Single-qubit phase: $R_Z(2x_i)$ applies data-dependent phases to each qubit $i$
  3. Two-qubit interactions: $ZZ(x_i x_j) = \text{CNOT}_{ij} \cdot (I \otimes R_Z(2 x_i x_j)) \cdot \text{CNOT}_{ij}$

The ZZ interactions encode pairwise feature products, enabling the quantum classifier to learn nonlinear decision boundaries. Because IQP circuits include entangling gates, they are:

  • NOT classically simulable (provably hard under standard assumptions)
  • Entangling (creates multi-qubit correlations)
  • Expressive (can access a large portion of the Hilbert space)
  • Subject to barren plateaus at high depth (trainability decreases with reps)

docs.title: 2. Creating an IQPEncoding¶
docs.text:
The IQPEncoding constructor accepts three parameters:

Parameter Type Default Description n_features int required Number of classical features to encode (also determines qubit count) reps int 2 Number of times to repeat the encoding layer entanglement "full", "linear", "circular" "full" Topology of ZZ interactions between qubits

docs.title: 2.1 Constructor Validation¶
docs.text: The constructor validates all parameters strictly. Let's verify each validation rule.

docs.title: 3. Core Properties¶
docs.text: IQPEncoding exposes several properties inherited from BaseEncoding plus its own attributes.

docs.title: 4. Encoding Properties (Lazy, Thread-Safe)¶
docs.text:
The properties attribute returns an EncodingProperties frozen dataclass. It is:

  • Lazily computed on first access (not at construction time)
  • Thread-safe via double-checked locking
  • Cached after first computation

docs.title: 5. Entanglement Pairs¶
docs.text:
IQPEncoding uses ZZ interactions between qubit pairs. The topology determines which pairs interact:

Topology Pairs Count Connectivity full All (i, j) with i < j n(n-1)/2 All-to-all linear (i, i+1) only n-1 Nearest-neighbor circular Linear + (n-1, 0) for n>2 n (for n>2) Ring

docs.title: 6. Gate Count Breakdown¶
docs.text:
gate_count_breakdown() returns a GateCountBreakdown TypedDict with detailed gate counts:

Key Description hadamard H gates (n_qubits x reps) rz_single Single-qubit RZ gates for data encoding rz_zz RZ gates in ZZ interaction decomposition cnot CNOT gates (2 x n_pairs x reps) total_single_qubit hadamard + rz_single + rz_zz total_two_qubit cnot count total total_single_qubit + total_two_qubit

docs.title: 7. Resource Summary¶
docs.text: resource_summary() provides a comprehensive overview of the encoding's resource requirements.

docs.title: 8. Circuit Generation -- PennyLane Backend¶
docs.text: PennyLane is the default backend. get_circuit() returns a callable (closure) that applies quantum gates when invoked inside a qml.QNode context.

docs.title: 9. Circuit Generation -- Qiskit Backend¶
docs.text: The Qiskit backend returns a QuantumCircuit object that can be visualized, transpiled, or executed on real hardware.

docs.title: 10. Circuit Generation -- Cirq Backend¶
docs.text: The Cirq backend returns a cirq.Circuit object with Moment objects.

docs.title: 11. Entanglement Topology Comparison (Full vs Linear vs Circular)¶
docs.text:
The entanglement topology fundamentally changes the quantum state structure, gate count, and expressivity.

Topology Gate Scaling Connectivity Best For full O(n^2) All-to-all Maximum expressivity linear O(n) Nearest-neighbor NISQ hardware circular O(n) Ring Periodic boundary problems

docs.title: 12. Repetitions (reps) -- Effect on Depth, Gates, and Properties¶
docs.text: Unlike AngleEncoding where reps simply multiplies the rotation angle, IQP encoding repeats the entire layer structure (H + RZ + ZZ) reps times, creating deeper entanglement.

docs.title: 13. Batch Circuit Generation¶
docs.text: get_circuits() generates circuits for multiple data samples at once, with optional parallel processing.

docs.title: 14. Input Validation & Edge Cases¶
docs.text: IQPEncoding performs thorough input validation. This section demonstrates every validation rule.

docs.title: 15. Resource Analysis¶
docs.text: The encoding_atlas.analysis module provides tools for comparing and estimating encoding resources.

docs.title: 16. Simulability Analysis¶
docs.text: IQPEncoding produces entangled states, making it not classically simulable under standard complexity-theoretic assumptions.

docs.title: 17. Expressibility Analysis¶
docs.text: Expressibility measures how well an encoding can explore the Hilbert space compared to Haar-random states. IQP encoding is expected to be more expressive than non-entangling encodings like AngleEncoding.

docs.title: 18. Entanglement Capability¶
docs.text: IQPEncoding creates entangled states. The entanglement capability should be significantly greater than zero.

docs.title: 19. Trainability Analysis¶
docs.text: IQP encoding's trainability decreases with depth (reps) due to the entangling nature of the circuit. Deep IQP circuits may exhibit barren plateaus.

docs.title: 20. Low-Level Utilities¶
docs.text: The encoding_atlas.analysis module provides low-level utilities for custom analysis.

docs.title: 21. Capability Protocols¶
docs.text: The library uses Python's structural subtyping (PEP 544) to define optional capability protocols. IQPEncoding implements both ResourceAnalyzable and EntanglementQueryable, but NOT DataDependentResourceAnalyzable or DataTransformable.

docs.title: 22. Registry System¶
docs.text: IQPEncoding is registered in the global encoding registry under the name "iqp", enabling factory-style creation.

docs.title: 23. Equality, Hashing & Serialization¶
docs.text: IQPEncoding supports equality comparison, hashing (usable in sets/dicts), and full pickle serialization.

docs.title: 24. Thread Safety¶
docs.text: IQPEncoding is designed for safe concurrent use. Circuit generation is stateless, and properties use double-checked locking.

docs.title: 25. Logging & Debugging¶
docs.text: IQPEncoding uses Python's standard logging module for debugging.

docs.title: 26. Full Entanglement Warning¶
docs.text: When using entanglement='full' with more than 12 features, a UserWarning is issued because the circuit complexity may exceed NISQ device limits.

docs.title: 27. Encoding Recommendation Guide¶
docs.text: The library includes a recommendation guide that suggests encodings based on problem characteristics.

docs.title: 28. Visualization & Comparison¶
docs.text: Compare IQPEncoding against other encodings to understand its trade-offs.

docs.title: 29. Putting It All Together -- Complete Workflow¶
docs.text: A realistic end-to-end example: select, configure, analyze, and use IQPEncoding for a quantum machine learning task using the Iris dataset.

docs.title: Summary¶
docs.text: This notebook demonstrated every feature of IQPEncoding from the Quantum Encoding Atlas library:

docs.title: Core Features¶
docs.text:
• Construction with n_features, reps, and entanglement (full/linear/circular) parameters
  • Strict validation of all constructor arguments and input data
  • Core properties: n_qubits, depth (= 3 * reps), n_features, config, repr
  • Lazy, thread-safe properties via EncodingProperties frozen dataclass
  • Entanglement pairs: Full (O(n^2)), linear (O(n)), circular (O(n))

docs.title: Multi-Backend Circuit Generation¶
docs.text:
• PennyLane: Returns callable closure for QNode integration
  • Qiskit: Returns QuantumCircuit object
  • Cirq: Returns cirq.Circuit with parallel moments

docs.title: Analysis Capabilities¶
docs.text:
• Resource analysis: gate_count_breakdown(), resource_summary(), count_resources(), compare_resources(), estimate_execution_time()
  • Simulability: Always "not_simulable" (provably hard classically)
  • Expressibility: High (entangling circuits access more of the Hilbert space)
  • Entanglement: Non-zero (ZZ interactions create multi-qubit correlations)
  • Trainability: Moderate, decreasing with depth (barren plateau risk)

docs.title: Low-Level Utilities¶
docs.text:
• Statevector simulation, fidelity, purity, entropy computation
  • Partial trace for reduced density matrices
  • Random parameter generation and RNG control

docs.title: Software Engineering Features¶
docs.text:
• Capability protocols: ResourceAnalyzable and EntanglementQueryable (PEP 544)
  • Registry system: Factory-style creation via get_encoding("iqp")
  • Equality and hashing: Usable in sets and dicts
  • Pickle serialization: Full round-trip with lock recreation
  • Thread safety: Concurrent circuit generation and property access
  • Debug logging: Granular logging for troubleshooting
  • Full entanglement warning: UserWarning when n_features > 12

docs.title: Key Properties of IQPEncoding¶
docs.text: Property Value Qubits n (one per feature) Depth 3 * reps Gate count reps * (2n + 3 * n_pairs) Two-qubit gates 2 * n_pairs * reps Entangling Yes Simulable No (provably hard) Trainability max(0.3, 0.9 - 0.1 * reps) Hardware connectivity all-to-all (full), linear, or ring (circular)

# Writing generic code using protocols
def analyze_encoding(enc: BaseEncoding) -> dict:
    """Analyze any encoding using its declared capabilities."""
    result = {"name": enc.__class__.__name__, "n_qubits": enc.n_qubits}

    if isinstance(enc, ResourceAnalyzable):
        summary = enc.resource_summary()
        result["total_gates"] = summary["gate_counts"]["total"]
        result["is_entangling"] = summary["is_entangling"]

    if isinstance(enc, EntanglementQueryable):
        result["n_pairs"] = len(enc.get_entanglement_pairs())

    return result

docs.title: 1. Overview & Mathematical Background¶
docs.text: The PauliFeatureMap encodes classical data into quantum states using configurable Pauli rotation gates. It generalizes simpler encodings like ZZFeatureMap by allowing users to specify which Pauli terms to include.

docs.title: Circuit Structure (per repetition)¶
docs.text:
1. Hadamard Layer: $H^{\otimes n}$ creates uniform superposition
  2. Single-Qubit Pauli Rotations: $R_P(2x_i)$ for each feature $x_i$ and Pauli $P \in \{X, Y, Z\}$
  3. Two-Qubit Pauli Interactions: $\exp\left(-i\frac{\phi}{2} P_a \otimes P_b\right)$ for qubit pairs

docs.title: Feature Mapping Functions¶
docs.text:
• Single-qubit: $\phi(x_i) = 2 x_i$
  • Two-qubit: $\phi(x_i, x_j) = 2(\pi - x_i)(\pi - x_j)$

docs.title: Two-Qubit Gate Decomposition¶
docs.text:
Two-qubit Pauli rotations are decomposed as:

$$\exp\left(-i\frac{\phi}{2} P_a \otimes P_b\right) = \text{BasisChange} \cdot \text{CNOT} \cdot R_Z(\phi) \cdot \text{CNOT} \cdot \text{BasisChange}^\dagger$$

The basis change depends on the Pauli type:

  • Z: No change (computational basis)
  • X: Hadamard gate
  • Y: $S^\dagger \cdot H$ (rotate to Y-basis)

docs.title: References¶
docs.text:
• Havlíček, V., et al. (2019). "Supervised learning with quantum-enhanced feature spaces." Nature, 567(7747), 209-212.
  • Schuld, M., & Killoran, N. (2019). "Quantum Machine Learning in Feature Hilbert Spaces." Physical Review Letters, 122(4), 040504.

docs.title: 3. Creating a PauliFeatureMap¶
docs.text: The simplest way to create a PauliFeatureMap requires only the number of features. All other parameters have sensible defaults.

docs.title: 4.1 Pauli Terms¶
docs.text:
The paulis parameter controls which rotation gates are applied.

Valid single-qubit terms: "X", "Y", "Z" (applied to every qubit)

Valid two-qubit terms: "XX", "YY", "ZZ", "XY", "XZ", "YZ", "YX", "ZX", "ZY" (applied to entangled pairs)

Pauli Gate Overhead Notes Z Minimal Native on most hardware X Low (1 H gate) Requires basis change Y Medium (H + S) Requires two basis change gates ZZ 2 CNOTs Standard for IQP/ZZFeatureMap XX 2 CNOTs + 4 H Basis change adds 4 single-qubit gates YY 2 CNOTs + 8 gates Most overhead due to Y-basis changes

docs.title: 4.2 Repetitions (reps)¶
docs.text: The reps parameter controls the number of encoding layers. More repetitions increase expressibility but also circuit depth.

docs.title: 4.3 Entanglement Topologies¶
docs.text:
Three entanglement patterns control how two-qubit gates are connected:

Topology Gate Scaling Connectivity Best For "full" $O(n^2)$ All-to-all Max expressivity "linear" $O(n)$ Nearest-only NISQ devices "circular" $O(n)$ Ring Periodic problems

docs.title: 5. Core Properties & Attributes¶
docs.text: Every PauliFeatureMap instance exposes several properties.

docs.title: 6. Entanglement Pair Inspection¶
docs.text: get_entanglement_pairs() returns the list of qubit pairs that will have two-qubit interactions. This is useful for understanding circuit structure and verifying hardware connectivity requirements.

docs.title: 7. Circuit Generation Across Backends¶
docs.text: PauliFeatureMap supports three quantum computing frameworks: PennyLane, Qiskit, and Cirq. Each produces an equivalent circuit in the framework's native format.

docs.title: 8. Batch Circuit Generation & Parallel Processing¶
docs.text: get_circuits() generates circuits for multiple data samples at once. It supports parallel processing for large batches.

docs.title: Gate Count Breakdown¶
docs.text: gate_count_breakdown() provides an exact count of every gate type in the circuit.

docs.title: Resource Summary¶
docs.text: resource_summary() provides a comprehensive report including circuit structure, gate counts, encoding characteristics, and hardware requirements.

docs.title: 10. EncodingProperties & Lazy Evaluation¶
docs.text: The properties attribute returns a frozen EncodingProperties dataclass. It is lazily computed on first access and then cached (thread-safe via double-checked locking).

docs.title: 11. Capability Protocols (isinstance Checks)¶
docs.text: The library uses Python's structural subtyping (PEP 544 Protocols) to declare optional capabilities. PauliFeatureMap implements ResourceAnalyzable and EntanglementQueryable.

docs.title: 12. Analysis Tools¶
docs.text: The encoding_atlas.analysis module provides comprehensive analysis functions.

docs.title: 12.2 Simulability Analysis¶
docs.text: Determines whether the encoding can be efficiently simulated classically.

docs.title: 12.3 Expressibility¶
docs.text: Measures how well the encoding explores the Hilbert space. Higher values (closer to 1.0) indicate the encoding produces states closer to the Haar-random distribution.

docs.title: 12.4 Entanglement Capability¶
docs.text: Measures how much entanglement the encoding generates using the Meyer-Wallach measure. Value ranges from 0 (product states) to 1 (maximally entangled).

docs.title: 12.5 Trainability & Barren Plateau Detection¶
docs.text: Estimates how easy it is to optimize parameters through the encoding (relevant for variational quantum algorithms).

docs.title: 13. Statevector Simulation & Quantum State Inspection¶
docs.text: The analysis utilities let you simulate the encoding to get the output quantum state.

docs.title: 14. Equality, Hashing & Serialization¶
docs.text: PauliFeatureMap supports equality comparison, hashing, and pickle serialization.

docs.title: 15. Configuration Access & Read-Only Safety¶
docs.text: The config property returns a read-only copy of the configuration dictionary.

docs.title: 16. Input Validation & Edge Cases¶
docs.text: PauliFeatureMap includes comprehensive input validation at both construction time and circuit generation time.

docs.title: 17. Logging & Warnings¶
docs.text: PauliFeatureMap uses Python's logging module for debugging and warnings for user-facing alerts.

docs.title: 18. Comparison with Related Encodings¶
docs.text: PauliFeatureMap generalizes several other encodings in the library.

docs.title: 19. Registry System¶
docs.text: The library includes a registry system to discover and instantiate encodings by name.

docs.title: 20. Hardware Planning Guide¶
docs.text: PauliFeatureMap provides all the information needed for hardware-aware circuit design.

docs.title: Key Takeaways¶
docs.text:
• PauliFeatureMap is the most configurable encoding in the library, allowing arbitrary combinations of Pauli rotation terms.
  • With default settings ["Z", "ZZ"], it behaves identically to ZZFeatureMap.
  • Three entanglement topologies trade off between expressivity (full) and hardware compatibility (linear, circular).
  • The library provides comprehensive analysis tools for expressibility, entanglement, trainability, simulability, and resources.
  • All backends (PennyLane, Qiskit, Cirq) produce equivalent quantum states.
  • Thread-safe design enables parallel batch processing.
  • Extensive input validation catches errors early with clear messages.

# Linear vs quadratic feature mapping
x = np.array([0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0])

for fm in ["linear", "quadratic"]:
    enc = QAOAEncoding(n_features=4, gamma=1.0, feature_map=fm)
    angles = enc.compute_data_angles(x)
    print(f"feature_map='{fm:10s}' -> angles={np.round(angles, 4)}")
    # Verify: linear -> gamma*x, quadratic -> gamma*x^2
    if fm == "linear":
        expected = 1.0 * x
    else:
        expected = 1.0 * x**2
    assert np.allclose(angles, expected), "Mismatch!"
    print(f"  Verified: {'gamma*x' if fm == 'linear' else 'gamma*x^2'} = {np.round(expected, 4)}")

# Use within a PennyLane QNode to get statevector
try:
    import pennylane as qml

    dev = qml.device("default.qubit", wires=enc.n_qubits)

    @qml.qnode(dev)
    def run_circuit():
        circuit_fn()
        return qml.state()

    state = run_circuit()
    print(f"\nStatevector dimension: {len(state)}")
    print(f"State norm: {np.linalg.norm(state):.6f}")
    print(f"First 4 amplitudes: {np.round(state[:4], 6)}")
except ImportError:
    print("PennyLane not available - skipping execution")

import threading

enc = QAOAEncoding(n_features=4, reps=2)
results = {}
errors = []

def worker(thread_id, x):
    try:
        # Properties are thread-safe (double-checked locking)
        props = enc.properties
        # Circuit generation is thread-safe (stateless)
        circuit = enc.get_circuit(x, backend="pennylane")
        results[thread_id] = (props.gate_count, callable(circuit))
    except Exception as e:
        errors.append((thread_id, str(e)))

# Launch concurrent threads

    x = np.random.rand(4) * np.pi
    t = threading.Thread(target=worker, args=(i, x))
    threads.append(t)
    t.start()

for t in threads:

docs.title: QAOAEncoding - Complete Feature Demonstration¶
docs.text:
A comprehensive guide to every feature of QAOAEncoding in the encoding-atlas library.

This notebook demonstrates the full capabilities of the QAOA-style quantum data encoding, covering:

  1. Installation & Setup - Getting started with the library
  2. Core Concepts - What QAOA encoding is and why it matters
  3. Instantiation & Configuration - All 10 constructor parameters
  4. Circuit Generation - PennyLane, Qiskit, and Cirq backends
  5. Batch Processing - Sequential and parallel circuit generation
  6. Properties & Resource Analysis - Gate counts, depth, simulability
  7. Entanglement Topologies - Linear, circular, full, none
  8. Feature Mapping - Linear vs quadratic mappings
  9. Data Angle Computation - Understanding rotation angles
  10. Serialization - to_dict, from_dict, pickle support
  11. Copy & Variation - Creating encoding variants
  12. Equality & Hashing - Comparison and set/dict usage
  13. Protocol Support - ResourceAnalyzable, EntanglementQueryable
  14. Analysis Tools - Expressibility, entanglement, trainability, simulability
  15. Visualization & Comparison - Comparing QAOA with other encodings
  16. Edge Cases & Validation - Input validation, warnings, error handling
  17. Advanced Usage - Logging, thread safety, hardware considerations
  18. End-to-End Workflow - Complete ML pipeline example

Mathematical Background:

The QAOA-style encoding creates quantum states through alternating layers inspired by the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm:

$$|\psi(x)\rangle = \prod_{p=1}^{\text{reps}} U_M(\beta) \, U_C(\gamma, x) \, |+\rangle^{\otimes n}$$

where:

  • $U_C(\gamma, x) = \prod_i R_{\text{data}}(\gamma \cdot x_i)$ applies data-dependent rotations
  • $U_M(\beta) = U_{\text{entangle}} \cdot \prod_i R_{\text{mixer}}(\beta)$ applies mixing operations
  • $|+\rangle^{\otimes n}$ is the uniform superposition state (when include_initial_h=True)

References:

  • Farhi, E., Goldstone, J., & Gutmann, S. (2014). "A Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm." arXiv:1411.4028.
  • Hadfield, S., et al. (2019). "From the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm to a Quantum Alternating Operator Ansatz."
  • Lloyd, S., et al. (2020). "Quantum embeddings for machine learning." arXiv:2001.03622.

docs.title: What is QAOA Encoding?¶
docs.text:
QAOA Encoding adapts the structure of the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm for classical data encoding into quantum states. Instead of optimizing a cost Hamiltonian, it uses data-dependent rotations to create rich quantum feature maps.

Circuit structure per repetition:

  1. Data encoding layer (cost layer): $R_{\text{data}}(\gamma \cdot x_i)$ on each qubit
  2. Mixer layer: $R_{\text{mixer}}(\beta)$ rotations + entangling gates

Why use QAOA encoding?

  • Problems with graph or combinatorial structure
  • Variational quantum classifiers
  • Quantum kernel methods requiring QAOA-like feature maps
  • Highly configurable (10 parameters) for fine-tuning

docs.title: 3. Instantiation - All 10 Constructor Parameters¶
docs.text: QAOAEncoding has 10 constructor parameters, each controlling a different aspect of the encoding. Let's explore every single one.

docs.title: 3.1 n_features (required) - Number of classical features¶
docs.text: Maps directly to the number of qubits: n_qubits = n_features.

docs.title: 3.2 reps (default=2) - Number of QAOA-style repetitions¶
docs.text: Controls the depth and expressibility of the encoding. Analogous to 'p' in QAOA literature.

docs.title: 3.3 data_rotation (default='Z') - Rotation axis for data encoding¶
docs.text: Controls which Pauli rotation gate encodes the data: RX, RY, or RZ.

docs.title: 3.4 mixer_rotation (default='X') - Rotation axis for mixer layer¶
docs.text: Controls the mixer Hamiltonian approximation. Standard QAOA uses RX (transverse field mixer).

docs.title: 3.5 entanglement (default='linear') - Entanglement topology¶
docs.text:
Four options controlling how qubits interact:

  • 'linear': Nearest-neighbor pairs (i, i+1) - hardware-friendly
  • 'circular': Linear + wrap-around (n-1, 0) - periodic boundary
  • 'full': All pairs (i, j) where i < j - maximum entanglement
  • 'none': No entanglement - product state encoding

docs.title: 3.6 entangling_gate (default='cz') - Type of entangling gate¶
docs.text:
Three options for the two-qubit entangling operation:

  • 'cx': CNOT gates
  • 'cz': Controlled-Z gates (symmetric, hardware-native on many platforms)
  • 'rzz': RZZ gates with angle beta (parameterized entanglement)

docs.title: 3.7 gamma (default=1.0) - Scaling factor for data encoding¶
docs.text: Controls the rotation angle: angle = gamma * x_i (linear) or gamma * x_i^2 (quadratic).

docs.title: 3.8 beta (default=1.0) - Scaling factor for mixer rotations¶
docs.text: Controls the mixer rotation angle. For RZZ gates, also controls the entangling interaction strength.

docs.title: 3.9 include_initial_h (default=True) - Initial Hadamard layer¶
docs.text:
Controls whether Hadamard gates create uniform superposition at the start.

  • True: Start from |+>^n (standard QAOA)
  • False: Start from |0>^n

docs.title: 3.10 feature_map (default='linear') - Feature mapping type¶
docs.text:
Controls how features map to rotation angles:

  • 'linear': phi(x_i) = gamma * x_i (direct mapping)
  • 'quadratic': phi(x_i) = gamma * x_i^2 (nonlinear mapping)

docs.title: Full Parameter Showcase¶
docs.text: Creating an encoding with every parameter explicitly specified:

docs.title: 4. Circuit Generation - All Three Backends¶
docs.text: QAOAEncoding supports three quantum computing frameworks: PennyLane, Qiskit, and Cirq.

docs.title: 4.1 PennyLane Backend¶
docs.text: Returns a callable function that applies gates when invoked within a QNode context.

docs.title: 4.2 Qiskit Backend¶
docs.text: Returns a QuantumCircuit object with barriers between repetitions for clarity.

docs.title: 4.3 Cirq Backend¶
docs.text: Returns a cirq.Circuit with optimized Moment structure for minimal depth. CZ and RZZ gates are parallelized into Moments; CNOT gates are applied sequentially.

docs.title: 4.4 Cross-Backend Consistency¶
docs.text: All backends produce the same quantum state for the same input.

docs.title: 5. Batch Circuit Generation¶
docs.text: Generate circuits for multiple data samples at once, with optional parallel processing.

docs.title: 5.2 Parallel Batch Processing¶
docs.text: Use parallel=True for large batches. Thread-safe because circuit generation is stateless.

docs.title: 6.1 EncodingProperties - Immutable Property Container¶
docs.text: Every encoding lazily computes theoretical properties (thread-safe).

docs.title: 7. Entanglement Topologies - Deep Dive¶
docs.text: The entanglement pattern has a major impact on encoding expressibility, circuit depth, and hardware requirements.

docs.title: 7.1 Depth Scaling by Entanglement Pattern¶
docs.text:
The depth of the entangling layer depends on the pattern and uses graph-theoretic optimal scheduling:

  • Linear: min(2, n-1) layers (even/odd pair parallelization)
  • Circular: 2 for even n, 3 for odd n (cycle graph edge coloring)
  • Full: n-1 for even n, n for odd n (complete graph chromatic index, Vizing's theorem)

docs.title: 9. Data Angle Computation¶
docs.text: The compute_data_angles() method reveals the rotation angles used in the data encoding layer.

docs.title: 10.2 Pickle Serialization¶
docs.text: All encodings support pickling, including cached properties. Thread locks are excluded from serialization and recreated on unpickling.

docs.title: 11. Copy & Variation¶
docs.text: Create encoding variants without modifying the original using copy().

docs.title: 12. Equality & Hashing¶
docs.text: QAOAEncoding supports equality comparison and hashing, enabling use in sets and as dict keys.

docs.title: 13. Capability Protocols¶
docs.text: QAOAEncoding implements two capability protocols from the library's Layered Contract Architecture.

docs.title: 14. Analysis Tools¶
docs.text: The encoding_atlas.analysis module provides quantitative analysis capabilities.

docs.title: 14.3 Expressibility Analysis¶
docs.text: Measures how well the encoding covers the Hilbert space by comparing its fidelity distribution to the Haar random distribution.

docs.title: 14.4 Entanglement Capability¶
docs.text: Measures the encoding's ability to generate entanglement using Meyer-Wallach and Scott measures.

docs.title: 17. Edge Cases & Input Validation¶
docs.text: The library provides thorough input validation with helpful error messages.

docs.title: 17.7 Warning: Full Entanglement with Many Features¶
19. Exception Hierarchy¶
docs.text: The library provides a rich exception hierarchy for precise error handling.

# Step 1: Encode x -> |psi(x)>
state_x = enc._encode_state(x)
print("Step 1 - |psi(x)>:")
for i, amp in enumerate(state_x):
    if abs(amp) > 1e-10:
        print(f"  |{i:02b}> : {amp:.6f}")

# Step 2: Apply U(phi) to |psi(x)>
U_phi = enc.unitary_representation(phi)
left_side = U_phi @ state_x
print(f"\nStep 2 - U(phi)|psi(x)>:")
for i, amp in enumerate(left_side):
    if abs(amp) > 1e-10:
        print(f"  |{i:02b}> : {amp:.6f}")

# Step 3: Rotate x, then encode -> |psi(rotate(x, phi))>
x_rotated = enc.group_action(phi, x)
print(f"\nStep 3a - Rotated point: [{x_rotated[0]:.6f}, {x_rotated[1]:.6f}]")

right_side = enc._encode_state(x_rotated)
print(f"Step 3b - |psi(rotate(x, phi))>:")
for i, amp in enumerate(right_side):
    if abs(amp) > 1e-10:
        print(f"  |{i:02b}> : {amp:.6f}")

# Step 4: Compare (up to global phase)
overlap = np.abs(np.vdot(left_side, right_side))

docs.title: SO2EquivariantFeatureMap: Complete Feature Demonstration¶
docs.text:
This notebook provides a comprehensive walkthrough of the SO2EquivariantFeatureMap encoding from the Quantum Encoding Atlas library. This encoding is equivariant to 2D rotations, satisfying the mathematical property:

$$U(\phi)|\psi(r, \theta)\rangle = |\psi(r, \theta + \phi)\rangle$$

where $(r, \theta)$ are polar coordinates of a 2D point and $\phi$ is a rotation angle.

The encoding maps 2D Cartesian data into quantum states using angular momentum eigenstates:

$$|\psi(r, \theta)\rangle = \sum_{m} c_m(r) \cdot e^{im\theta} |m\rangle$$

where:

  • $m \in \{-\text{max\_m}, \ldots, +\text{max\_m}\}$ are angular momentum quantum numbers
  • $c_m(r)$ are radial amplitude functions (rotation-invariant)
  • $e^{im\theta}$ encodes the angle as phases
  • $|m\rangle$ are angular momentum basis states

docs.title: 2. Instantiation & Constructor Validation¶
docs.text: The SO2EquivariantFeatureMap enforces strict mathematical constraints. SO(2) rotation equivariance requires exactly 2D input (Cartesian coordinates [x, y]).

docs.title: 2.3 Validation: n_features Must Be Exactly 2¶
docs.text: This is a fundamental mathematical constraint: SO(2) rotation equivariance is defined for 2D data.

docs.title: 3. Core Properties & Configuration¶
docs.text: Every encoding exposes its configuration and computed properties.

docs.title: 4. Angular Momentum Basis & State Encoding¶
docs.text: The SO(2) encoding uses angular momentum eigenstates as the computational basis. Understanding this mapping is key to understanding how equivariance works.

docs.title: 4.1 Spin-1 Triplet Basis (max_angular_momentum=1)¶
docs.text:
For max_angular_momentum=1 with 2 qubits, the encoding uses the spin-1 triplet states:

| Angular Momentum $m$ | Basis State $|m\rangle$ | |---|---| | $m = +1$ | $|00\rangle$ | | $m = 0$ | $(|01\rangle + |10\rangle)/\sqrt{2}$ | | $m = -1$ | $|11\rangle$ |

docs.title: 4.3 State Encoding: Polar Decomposition¶
docs.text:
The encoding converts Cartesian $(x, y)$ to polar $(r, \theta)$, then builds:

$$|\psi(r, \theta)\rangle = \sum_m c_m(r) \cdot e^{im\theta} |m\rangle$$

docs.title: 5. Circuit Generation (Multi-Backend)¶
docs.text: The encoding supports three quantum computing backends: PennyLane, Qiskit, and Cirq.

docs.title: 6. Batch Circuit Generation¶
docs.text: The get_circuits method generates circuits for multiple data samples at once, with optional parallel processing.

docs.title: 7. SO(2) Group Actions & Unitary Representation¶
docs.text: The SO(2) group consists of 2D rotations. The encoding provides methods to apply group actions to both classical data and quantum states.

docs.title: 8. Equivariance Verification¶
docs.text:
The core mathematical property: rotating the input is equivalent to applying the rotation operator on the quantum state.

$$U(\phi)|\psi(x)\rangle = |\psi(\text{rotate}(x, \phi))\rangle$$

docs.title: 8.5 Manual Equivariance Verification (Step by Step)¶
docs.text: Let's manually verify the equivariance condition: $U(\phi)|\psi(x)\rangle = |\psi(\text{rotate}(x, \phi))\rangle$

docs.title: 9. Statistical Equivariance Verification¶
docs.text: For larger systems where exact statevector comparison is infeasible, the encoding provides a measurement-based statistical test using chi-squared analysis.

docs.title: 10. Resource Analysis & Gate Counts¶
docs.text: The encoding provides comprehensive resource analysis for hardware planning.

docs.title: 11. Capability Protocols¶
docs.text: The Encoding Atlas uses a layered contract architecture with runtime-checkable protocols.

docs.title: 12. Radial Functions: Gaussian vs Uniform¶
docs.text: The radial function $c_m(r)$ controls how the radius is encoded in state amplitudes.

docs.title: 13. Varying Angular Momentum¶
docs.text: The max_angular_momentum parameter controls the encoding's expressiveness and qubit requirements.

docs.title: 14. Edge Cases & Numerical Stability¶
docs.text: The encoding handles various edge cases gracefully.

docs.text: Let's compare the SO(2) equivariant encoding with other encodings in the library.

docs.title: Key Takeaways¶
docs.text: | Feature | Details | |---|---| | Symmetry Group | SO(2) - 2D rotations | | Input | 2D Cartesian coordinates [x, y] | | Equivariance | $U(\phi)|\psi(x)\rangle = |\psi(\text{rotate}(x, \phi))\rangle$ | | Parameters | max_angular_momentum, radial_function, radial_sigma | | Qubits | $\lceil\log_2(2 \cdot \text{max\_m} + 1)\rceil$ | | Backends | PennyLane, Qiskit, Cirq | | Verification | Exact (small systems), Statistical (scalable), Auto | | Thread Safety | Yes (double-checked locking for properties) | | Serialization | Pickle-compatible |

docs.title: When to Use SO2EquivariantFeatureMap¶
docs.text:
• Your data has 2D rotational symmetry (point clouds, images, molecular orientations)
  • You want provable symmetry preservation in the quantum encoding
  • You need rotation-equivariant feature extraction for quantum ML
  • You want reduced hypothesis space for better sample efficiency

docs.title: When NOT to Use¶
docs.text:
• Data has more than 2 features (consider projecting to 2D first)
  • No rotational symmetry in the problem
  • Need for approximate symmetry handling (this encoding is exact)

# The key physics insight: swapping the two jets shouldn't change the prediction.
